newsitem.title: USA: Kmart completes repayment of $1.2 billion loan.
newsitem.headline: Kmart completes repayment of $1.2 billion loan.

text.p: Kmart Corp., in another sign that its health is improving, said Thursday it has completed repayment of a $1.2 billion bank loan taken out last year to help the discount retailer avert a financial crisis.
The loan was not due until 1999, and the early repayment is a major step toward improving Kmart's junk-bond credit rating.

"At the time of the refinancing, Kmart said it intended to pay this obligation down within one year," Marvin Rich, Kmart's executive vice president of finance, planning and administration, said in a news release.
"These actions make good on that promise one quarter ahead of schedule, providing further evidence of continued improvement in Kmart's financial health."

Kmart took on the loan in June 1996 to help pay off real estate-related notes that allowed holders to demand immediate repayment when Kmart's credit rating fell below investment grade -- a move that analysts said in late 1995 could have forced the company to seek bankruptcy protection.

Standard & Poor's Corp. has said that Kmart needs to show consistent operating and profitability improvements in its core discount store operations before the ratings agency will raise its credit rating to investment grade.

Kmart used asset sales to pay off much of the loan, including $257 million in the sale of Rite-Aid Corp. stock, $335 million from a real estate transaction, and $74.25 million from the sale of its Mexican operations. The remainder came from operations and other minor asset-related transactions.
With repayment of the $1.2 billion loan, Kmart said its long-term debt is now only 35 percent of its total capitalisation, down from 51 percent at the end of 1995.

Kmart also said its interest costs are expected to fall in 1997, due both to a lower level of borrowings and lower anticipated interest rates on the Troy, Mich.-based company's $2.5 billion revolving credit facility.

The revolving credit facility itself, which is designed primarily to fund Kmart's short-term working capital needs, was entirely paid off in mid-December and remains untapped today, indicating stronger cash flows within the company's operations, Kmart said.
Kmart's stock fell 37.5 cents to $12.25 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
